Indignation
in-dig-NAY-shun
n.
Latin indignatio, “displeasure at what is unworthy,” from indignus (unworthy). Renders the Hebrew za‘am, “denunciation, indignation,” and the Greek aganaktēsis, “indignation,” and orge, “wrath,” in some uses.

📖 Biblical Definition

Indignation in Scripture is the burning displeasure of a holy mind at what is unworthy of God—at sin, at injustice, at the desecration of holy things, at the oppression of the weak, at every act that ought not to be. It belongs first to God, who is constantly named as indignant against iniquity and oppression; and it belongs derivatively to the regenerate saint, whose conformity to Christ includes a Spirit-wrought indignation at the very things God Himself is indignant against. Christ’s own indignation is on display in the Gospels. He looked round about on them with anger, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts; He was much displeased (the Greek is éganaktēsen, indignant) when the disciples kept the children from Him; He twice cleared the temple of the merchants with a zeal-driven indignation; He pronounced repeated woes upon the scribes and Pharisees whose religion oppressed the people. Paul commends the Corinthians for the Spirit-wrought indignation their repentance produced: for behold this selfsame thing, that ye sorrowed after a godly sort, what carefulness it wrought in you, yea, what clearing of yourselves, yea, what indignation, yea, what fear, yea, what vehement desire, yea, what zeal, yea, what revenge!—naming indignation as one of the seven marks of true repentance toward sin. The prophets are saturated with the holy indignation of the LORD at oppression, idolatry, and the perversion of justice; the Psalms cry out for indignation against the workers of iniquity and the enemies of God’s people; Revelation announces the final indignation that will pour out upon all unrighteousness at the day of the Lord. The biblical doctrine is therefore that holy indignation is a virtue, not a vice—but a virtue requiring the most careful guarding because it lies adjacent to its corruptions: personal anger that is merely fleshly resentment dressed in religious language, faction-driven outrage that has lost the calm clarity of God-shaped displeasure, and self-righteous indignation that condemns in others what it indulges in itself. The Christ-shaped indignation is grieved before it is angry, is directed at what God is indignant against and not at personal slights, is patient with the sinner even when sharp with the sin, and yields itself to the LORD’s appointed channels of address (church discipline, civil-authority appeal, prophetic speech) rather than venting itself in the flesh.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines INDIGNATION as anger or extreme anger, mingled with contempt, disgust or abhorrence; the wrath of God; in scripture, the holy displeasure of a regenerate mind at what is unworthy of God.

expand to see more

INDIGNATION, n. — 1. Anger or extreme anger, mingled with contempt, disgust or abhorrence. 2. The anger of a superior; extreme anger; particularly, the wrath of God against sinful men for their ingratitude and rebellion. 3. The effects of anger; the dreadful effects of God’s wrath; terrible judgments.

INDIGNANT, a. — Affected at once with anger and disdain; feeling the mingled emotions of wrath and scorn or contempt.

📖 Key Scripture

Mark 3:5 — "And when he had looked round about on them with anger, being grieved for the hardness of their hearts, he saith unto the man, Stretch forth thine hand..."

Mark 10:14 — "But when Jesus saw it, he was much displeased, and said unto them, Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God."

2 Corinthians 7:11 — "For behold this selfsame thing, that ye sorrowed after a godly sort, what carefulness it wrought in you, yea, what clearing of yourselves, yea, what indignation, yea, what fear..."

Psalm 7:11 — "God judgeth the righteous, and God is angry with the wicked every day."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Indignation is corrupted, on one side, by the therapeutic register that has trained the believer to suppress all righteous anger as toxic—and on the other by the online-outrage register that performs indignation chronically and at low cost, often venting personal resentment under the cover of moral seriousness.

expand to see more

The therapeutic suppression of indignation is the more recent contemporary corruption. The believer is taught that all anger is unhealthy, that righteous indignation is a contradiction in terms, and that the mature soul has transcended the very capacity for the displeasure Scripture commends as a mark of true repentance and a likeness to Christ. The text refuses this. Christ Himself was angry at the Pharisees’ hardness, displeased with the disciples’ obstruction of the children, indignant at the temple’s desecration; Paul lists indignation among the seven marks of godly sorrow that worketh repentance; the Psalms and Prophets are saturated with the LORD’s indignation at oppression and idolatry. To suppress all indignation is not Christian maturity; it is the loss of a Spirit-wrought disposition Scripture itself commends. Recover the doctrine, and the saint regains the capacity to be properly grieved and properly angry at what God Himself is grieved and angry about—and the moral seriousness the gospel produces returns to the regenerate soul.

The opposite corruption is the online-outrage register that performs indignation chronically and at low cost. The believer scrolls his feeds, identifies the issue of the day, posts the requisite indignant response, and feels he has done his part—often without any of the carefulness, fear, vehement desire, zeal, or revenge (against the sin in himself first) that Paul names as the proper concomitants of biblical indignation. The performance is cheap; the substance is missing; and the recurring practice trains the soul into a chronic outrage that wears the dress of moral seriousness but is often closer to personal resentment, faction-loyalty, or sheer habit. Recover the Christ-shaped pattern: indignation that is grieved before it is angry, directed at what God is indignant against, patient with the sinner even when sharp with the sin, yielded to the LORD’s appointed channels of address. Indignation rightly held is a virtue; indignation chronically performed online and never patiently embodied is the cheap counterfeit.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew za‘am (denunciation, indignation) and chemah (heat, wrath); Greek aganaktēsis (indignation) and orgē (settled wrath)—the holy displeasure of God at sin and oppression, and the Spirit-wrought derivative displeasure of the regenerate soul at what God Himself opposes.

expand to see more

Hebrew za‘am (H2195) — denunciation, indignation, anger.

Hebrew chemah (H2534) — heat, wrath, indignation.

Greek aganakteō (G23) — to be indignant (Mark 10:14; 14:4; Matt 20:24; 21:15; 26:8; Luke 13:14).

Greek aganaktēsis (G24) — indignation (2 Cor 7:11).

Usage

"Christ’s own indignation in the Gospels (the temple, the hardness of hearts, the obstruction of the children) shows the Spirit-wrought displeasure as a Christ-likeness, not a sin."

"What indignation—Paul names indignation as one of the seven marks of godly sorrow that worketh repentance."

"Therapeutic suppression empties the category; online-outrage performance counterfeits it; biblical indignation is Christ-shaped, patient, and yielded to the LORD’s appointed channels."
